title: Weeping and shouting (Ezra 3:10–13)
hookLine: at the new foundation the old weep and others shout, and no one can tell the sounds apart

cards: Two sounds rise from the same building site, and both are loud. The builders have just laid the foundation of the new house of the LORD in Jerusalem. The priests stand in their robes with trumpets.
The Levites, sons of Asaph, stand with cymbals. They sing back and forth, praising and giving thanks, in the King James words, "because he is good, for his mercy endureth for ever toward Israel."
The people answer with a great shout. It should be a simple, happy scene. It isn't simple.

teach.b: Here's what the text says next: "But many of the priests and Levites and chief of the fathers, who were ancient men, that had seen the first house, when the foundation of this house was laid before their eyes, wept with a loud voice; and many shouted aloud for joy."
The old men had seen the first Temple. Standing at the beginning of the second, they weep. The text doesn't say why.
Maybe grief for what was lost. Maybe the memory of what used to stand there. Maybe relief, after so long.
Maybe all of it at once.
And many others shout for joy at a beginning.

teach.h: NO ONE CAN TELL THE SOUNDS APART.
teach.b: Notice who is weeping: not doubters on the edge of the crowd, but priests and Levites, the same groups the text set at the center of the song, along with the heads of families.
Then: "So that the people could not discern the noise of the shout of joy from the noise of the weeping of the people." The text refuses to separate them.
It doesn't say the joy drowned out the tears, or that the old men should have cheered up.

teach.h: THE NOISE WAS HEARD AFAR OFF.
teach.b: Both sounds rise together, and the noise, it says, was heard afar off.
Anyone listening from a distance heard one sound, made of both.

how: At a Jewish wedding, by tradition, a glass is broken at the end of the ceremony, which some explain as remembering the destruction of Jerusalem even at a moment of great joy.

games.q: you're one of the old men at the foundation. you saw the first house standing. now trumpets sound, and the crowd shouts for joy. what does the text say you do?

leave the site before the singing ends.
games.why: the ancient men wept with a loud voice, and the shouts of joy rose with them, so no one could tell the sounds apart.

practice: Bring to mind one thing in your life that holds two sounds: a new job and an old one, a child growing up, a move, a loss that also made room.
Let both be there, the way the noise at the foundation was heard as one, without choosing which wins. If you pray, bring both to God in words from your tradition.

wordCard.voice: Asaph, whose sons the Levites stood with cymbals as the Temple's new foundation was praised with weeping and shouting at once. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: weeping, from Ezra 3:13, where the weeping of the people can't be told from the shout of joy.

carryVoice: Your line: weeping and joy together. Neither sound cancels the other; from afar, they were one. See you tomorrow.
